title: Tenant peering and safety layers PRD draft
body:
Purpose and intent:

This doc captures an early PRD-level sketch for two complementary features aimed at improving Dedicated capacity behavior under transient load: (1) Tenant Peering Lanes — a controlled mechanism where trusted tenants can share ephemeral spare capacity under carefully defined policies, and (2) Safety Layers for bursts — a multi-tier safety architecture (policy + runtime) that prevents noisy neighbors and protects SLO budgets while preserving useful burst behavior.

Context and motivation:
- We get recurring asks for larger burst headroom for a subset of customers during predictable events (demos, launches) without forcing larger reserved commitments.
- Existing burst credit pools and soft-reservation mechanisms are helpful, but they either expose us to SLO risk or require heavy manual ops to configure tenant-by-tenant.
- Some customers (platform teams, internal teams, strategic beta partners) are willing to accept tighter isolation or pay premium for reciprocal peering; this enables higher utilization if we can guarantee safety.

Goals (success metrics):
- Maintain 99.9th percentile p99 response latency within existing SLO for primary tenants on a pool during a peering event (SLO degradation < 10% of baseline).
- Reduce unused reserved capacity in pilot pools by 8–12% by allowing controlled peering over a 3-month pilot.
- No customer-visible data plane errors > 0.05% of requests attributable to peering or burst reclaim operations.
- Operational readiness: runbook executes full emergency reclaim in < 3 minutes with safe rollbacks.

High-level product concepts:
1) Tenant Peering Lanes (TPL)
- Definition: a configurable policy object attached to a Dedicated pool that allows pre-approved tenants to consume ephemeral spare capacity when the pool has headroom, with prioritized fallback and repayment behavior.
- Policy knobs:
  * peering_role: lender | borrower | reciprocal
  * allowed_tenants: list of tenant IDs (for pilot this is explicit)
  * max_peering_share_pct: percent of unused pool capacity that can be borrowed (e.g., 15%)
  * priority_multiplier: numeric weight to resolve contention across borrowers
  * repayment_window: time window to gracefully return borrowed tokens or pay premium (1h/6h/24h)
  * charge_model: none | surcharge-per-token | offset-with-credit
- Runtime behavior: when pool utilization < threshold (pool_free_pct > configured threshold), system grants ephemeral tokens to borrowers. Tokens carry metadata for repayment and preemption priority.
- Preemption: tokens are soft-preemptible with staged reclaim (notify -> slow-warm-evict -> immediate-evict).

2) Safety Layers for bursts
- Layer 0: Admission controls — request-level quotas, concurrency limits, and per-route budgets (existing).
- Layer 1: Burst credit accounting — each tenant has burst credits capped and decayed by configurable half-life.
- Layer 2: Pool-level SLO protector — monitors aggregate p99, queue depth, and CPU/GPU tail metrics; triggers conservative throttles across low-priority tenants when thresholds hit.
- Layer 3: Emergency reclaim & shard fencing — rapid isolation where specific shards are fenced off and traffic redirected to permanent fallback models or regions.

APIs and configuration surfaces (product-facing):
- New REST endpoints and console controls:
  * POST /pools/{id}/peering-policy -> create/update TPL
  * GET /pools/{id}/peering-status -> live view of granted tokens and borrowers
  * POST /pools/{id}/safety-protector -> set SLO protector thresholds and actions
- Console UX: streamlined toggle to enable "pilot peering" with risk summary, estimated utilization uplift, and recommended max_peering_share_pct.

Autoscaler interactions:
- Autoscaler should be peering-aware: when scaling up (add nodes), peering borrowers get reduced priority to scale (i.e., autoscaler first ramps pool owner's reserved lanes).
- When autoscaler scales down, it only schedules decommissions from borrower allocations first (via token expiry) unless owner lanes are free.
- Predictive warm pools: use historical peering signals + calendar events to pre-warm capacity for expected borrower spikes with a neutral cost allocation.

Operational design and observability:
- New metrics to capture:
  * pool_peering_utilization_pct (by tenant)
  * peering_preemptions_count
  * peering_repayment_lag_seconds
  * slo_protector_trigger_count and impact_deltas (p50/p95/p99 before/after)
- Dashboards and alerts:
  * SLO Protector Alert: when p99 delta > configured buffer or queue depth crosses threshold -> auto throttle and page SRE.
  * Peering Health: trending of peering utilization and repayment queue > 5% -> Product/Eng review weekly.
- Runbook bullets:
  * Step 0: Observe SLO protector triggers in dashboard (automated)
  * Step 1: Pause new peering grants via control-plane flag
  * Step 2: Initiate staged reclaim for borrower tokens (notify webhook -> 60s -> 10s)
  * Step 3: If reclaim fails, fence shards and failover affected tenant to fallback model
  * Step 4: Postmortem and adjust max_peering_share_pct / repayment_window

Pricing & billing notes:
- For pilot we will offer peering as an opt-in premium: surcharge-per-token model (small multiplier on per-token cost during peering) or a credit-offset model where borrowers purchase "peering credits" at a discount.
- Accounting must track borrowed token usage separately for accurate billing and quota reconciliation.

Experiment plan and pilot scope:
- Phase 0 (internal alpha): internal Redwood tenant + 2 friendly beta customers; pool owners in US-west region; small scale (2 pools). Observe SLO impact for 1 month.
- Phase 1 (closed beta): 10 customers, add cost-model + UI flows. Metrics: utilization uplift, repayment lag, customer satisfaction.
- Phase 2 (general availability): gated on < 2 SLO incidents in last 90 days and integration of automated repayment reporting into billing.

Acceptance criteria for GA:
- Automated safeguards engage correctly on predefined stress tests (see linked experiment doc).
- Billing and reconciliation reports are accurate within 0.5% of token accounting.
- Runbook time-to-safe-state validated in 5 simulated bleed scenarios.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- Complexity vs. predictability: Introducing peering increases scheduling complexity; how much operational overhead can we tolerate?
- Cross-tenant economics: Should lenders receive economic incentives? If yes, how to avoid perverse incentives to artificially create spare capacity?
- Multi-region peering: do we allow cross-region borrow? Latency and data residency concerns may prohibit it initially.
- Refund semantics: if borrower repays late, do we charge penalties, or is repayment a soft contract?

Implementation notes (engineering pointers):
- Token design must be compact and distributed (k/v with TTL) and resilient across restarts.
- Integrate SLO protector with tracing to capture causal chain of latency increases (prefix cache hits, KV cache thrash, kernel stall events).
- Autoscaler hooks: add scoring layer to prefer owner lanes when scaling up.

Security and compliance considerations:
- Peering metadata must not leak tenant identifiers to other borrowers. Only control plane maintains mapping.
- For regulated customers, peering should be disallowed by default; enforce at policy creation time.

Appendix: quick examples and scenarios:
- Example policy JSON (conceptual): { peering_role: "borrower", allowed_tenants: ["t-acme"], max_peering_share_pct: "12", repayment_window: "6h", charge_model: "surcharge-per-token" }
- Scenario A: sudden demo spike for borrower; grant 10% pool capacity, p99 remains within 7% of baseline due to SLO protector; borrower billed surcharge 1.2x.
- Scenario B: flash spike that causes p99 noise -> SLO protector throttles borrower; staged reclaim recovers owner SLO within 90s, borrower sees throttled responses and fallback invocation.

Next steps / owners:
- Product: refine policy UX and pricing models (Ava Chen).
- Eng: prototype token store + peering grants in a sandbox pool (Diego Morales).
- SRE: define exact runbook timings and prepare synthetic tests (Nora Patel).
- Legal: quick review on commercial terms for pilot peering (Priya Kapoor).

Notes to self (rough):
- Link up with billing team early; token accounting is going to be painful if we try to bolt it on later.
- Keep initial allowed_tenants explicit - no discovery or broad permissioning for pilot.
- Consider a late-binding opt-in where lender gets small revenue share to align incentives.

References and experiments:
- linked: ENG-1327 (sim harness for staggered reclaim); Confluence TP-42 (peering legal checklist); GH PR 789 (autoscaler peering hooks).
